reading: *301 is a record or transaction label that opens or frames an administrative entry, not a counted commodity.
why: It appears on 230 nodules (administrative tags, not commodity tallies), it is almost never in first position on tablets (1 of 7, well below the base rate for commodity signs), and when it does carry a figure the largest is only 11 with fractions in only 17% of cases—consistent with an administrative label rather than a commodity being measured; crucially, it also attaches as a syllable to other signs (DA, I, MI), suggesting a functional/classificatory role rather than a commodity identity.
refuted_by: If *301 were found consistently in first position on tablets heading lists of commodities with summing totals below it, or if it appeared in species-by-sex lists or alongside VIR with large whole-number figures, the heading reading would be false.

reading: SI is a staple commodity, likely a plant product such as cyperus or a similar agricultural good, recorded in moderate whole-number quantities with fractions at the ordinary rate.
why: Fractions appear in 23% of figured entries, matching the corpus base rate for commodity signs (27%), consistent with a staple rather than a fine or bulk good; the largest figure is only 14, indicating moderate quantities typical of staples; it co-occurs repeatedly with CYP (7 times) and appears after CYP with a smaller sub-quantity figure in all 3 measurable cases, suggesting it is a secondary commodity measured out from or alongside cyperus consignments.
refuted_by: If SI were found with figures consistently in the hundreds, or if fractions were shown to be systematically absent across a larger sample, the staple reading would be undermined; equally, if SI were demonstrated to always precede a commodity sign as an attached syllable rather than standing independently with its own figure, it would be reclassified as a qualifier.

reading: RO is a syllabic sign added to commodity logograms to mark a subtype or grade, not itself a counted commodity.
why: It appears attached as an added syllable to other signs (*401, DA, ]TU) rather than standing alone with figures; it records a figure only once in 95 attestations (and that figure is small, 20), and it never opens a tablet (0 of 2), which rules out heading; the overwhelming support on nodules sealed by specific sealers suggests it tags batches rather than enumerates a commodity in its own right.
refuted_by: If RO were found repeatedly heading its own columns with substantial figures and fractions at the corpus base rate, or listed in species-by-sex or graded series independent of any host logogram, the qualifier reading would be false.

reading: ZE is a transaction or record label that opens or frames an administrative entry, not a commodity or party counted in its own right.
why: The largest figure recorded with ZE is 0, meaning it never actually carries a count; it appears overwhelmingly on nodules (46 of 47 attestations) rather than tablets, which fits a sealing label rather than a commodity entry; and it never appears in first position on the one tablet where it occurs, suggesting it functions as a tag or label attached to sealed consignments rather than as a line-item commodity.
refuted_by: If ZE were found heading a tablet entry with a substantial positive integer following it, or if it appeared in a species-by-sex list alongside livestock signs with counts, the heading reading would be falsified.

reading: A category of male persons distinguished from plain VIR by an added syllabic qualifier, counted in whole units and recorded in moderate to large numbers.
why: The base sign is VIR (the standard male-person logogram); figures reach 235 and fractions appear in only 1 of 20 cases (5%, far below the 27% commodity base rate), both hallmarks of person-counting; the ligature structure (VIR + added syllable) matches the Linear A practice of specifying a sub-class of persons by appending a qualifier to the base sign.
refuted_by: If the unit were found consistently following GRA or CYP as a sub-quantity with fractional amounts at or above the corpus base rate, that would indicate a commodity ration or measure rather than a class of persons.

reading: TA is a staple commodity, likely a plant-based foodstuff, recorded in modest whole-number quantities across multiple administrative sites.
why: The largest figure is only 6, consistent with medium-scale staple accounting rather than bulk grain; fractions appear in 1 of 8 figured entries (12%), which is below the ordinary rate but not absent, fitting a staple better than a fine commodity; it appears on both tablets and nodules across four sites, suggesting a routinely tracked commodity in a standard administrative network, and it follows GRA and CYP in sequence, placing it among plant staples.
refuted_by: If TA were found consistently with figures in the hundreds or thousands, or if it appeared exclusively as an addendum to another sign rather than as a free-standing entry, the staple reading would be undermined.

reading: *304 is a staple commodity—likely a solid agricultural product such as figs, olives, or a similar stored good—recorded in moderate quantities with fractions at the ordinary rate.
why: Fractions appear in 24% of attestations, matching the corpus base rate of 27% (consistent with staple, not bulk or fine); the largest figure is only 20, indicating moderate quantities typical of staples rather than bulk grain; it co-occurs overwhelmingly with GRA, OLIV, NI, and OLE-grade commodities, placing it firmly in the agricultural staple register, and it follows GRA or OLE in sequence with a smaller figure 8 of 14 times, suggesting it is a sub-quantity or secondary commodity within the same agricultural entry rather than a heading or total.
refuted_by: If *304 were found consistently preceding its figure in first position on tablets (approaching the 11% base rate or higher), or if its figures were shown to sum the entries above them, it would indicate a heading or total rather than a commodity; alternatively, if fractions were found to be systematically absent across a larger sample, reclassification as a bulk staple would be warranted.

reading: OLE+U is a graded variety or quality of oil, distinguished from plain OLE by the added syllable U, counted in bulk whole units with fractions at a low rate.
why: The base sign OLE is the standard oil logogram and the ligature OLE+U follows the pattern of graded liquid commodities marked by an added syllable; fractions appear in only 2 of 19 figured entries (11%), consistent with the liquid class (ordinary rate) rather than the fine class (high fractions) or bulk grain class (near-zero fractions); it co-occurs repeatedly with OLE, OLE+MI, and OLIV, a cluster that is exactly what is expected for a set of oil grades recorded together.
refuted_by: If OLE+U were found consistently heading tablets before any other entry, or if its figures were shown to sum the OLE and OLE+MI entries above it, it would be a heading or total rather than a commodity; alternatively, if the fraction rate rose well above the corpus base rate of 27% in a larger sample, a reclassification toward the fine class would be required.

reading: OLE+KI is a graded or typed variety of the oil commodity, distinguished from plain OLE by the added syllable KI, recorded in moderate quantities with fractions at a rate consistent with liquid commodities.
why: (1) The base sign is OLE, the standard oil logogram, and the ligature pattern (base + added syllable) matches the graded-liquid convention seen across the corpus. (2) Fractions appear in 33% of entries, close to the corpus base rate of 27%, which fits liquid commodities rather than bulk staples (where fractions are rare) or fine commodities (where fractions dominate). (3) It recurs in the same documents as OLE, OLIV, and OLE+MI—a cluster of oil-related signs—and follows OLE with a smaller figure in 4 of 5 cases, consistent with a sub-type or secondary grade of oil being recorded after the main oil entry.
refuted_by: If OLE+KI were found systematically in first position opening tablets, or consistently listed alongside VIR and person-counts rather than oil signs, or if its figures were shown to be whole-unit only with no fractions across a larger sample, the liquid-grade reading would be undermined.

reading: GRA+PA is a staple commodity, likely a variety or processed form of grain, recorded in moderate whole-number quantities with fractions at a below-average rate.
why: The base sign is GRA (grain), and the ligature pattern—an added syllable modifying a commodity sign—matches graded staple commodities; figures reach 62 with fractions in only 17% of attestations (below the 27% corpus base rate, consistent with a bulk-leaning staple rather than a fine commodity); it co-occurs repeatedly with GRA and OLIV, the core staple signs, and follows GRA in the entry order three times, suggesting it is a related but distinct grain category.
refuted_by: If GRA+PA were consistently found in fractional amounts at or above the corpus base rate (≥27%), or if it appeared exclusively with fine or liquid commodities rather than grain and olive signs, the staple reading would be undermined; equally, if future decipherment showed PA here functions as a qualifier on a non-grain base sign, the grain-variety interpretation would collapse.

reading: DI is a bulk staple commodity, most likely a grain or grain-like product recorded in whole units with figures up to 65.
why: Fractions appear in only 2 of 14 counted entries (14%), well below the corpus base rate of 27%, pointing to a bulk commodity rather than a fine or liquid one; the largest figure reaches 65, consistent with staple-scale quantities; it follows GRA twice and its figure is smaller than the preceding GRA figure in the one case where comparison is possible, suggesting it is a related sub-commodity or secondary grain product tallied after the main grain entry.
refuted_by: If future tablets showed DI consistently appearing with fractional amounts at or above the corpus base rate (≥27%), or if DI were found opening documents in first position at the base rate, the bulk classification would be undermined.

reading: RE is a staple commodity, likely a foodstuff or agricultural product counted in moderate whole quantities alongside grain and wine.
why: Fractions appear in only 8% of attestations (below the corpus base rate of 27%, but not negligible), the largest figure is 104 (moderate, consistent with staple-scale quantities), and it co-occurs repeatedly with GRA and VIN—the core staple and liquid commodities—following them in sequence, suggesting it belongs to the same accounting register.
refuted_by: If RE were found heading tablets at a rate near the base rate (11%) or consistently preceding rather than following commodity logograms, it would suggest a heading or qualifier role rather than a commodity entry; alternatively, if figures attached to RE were consistently small and fractional, a reclassification as a fine commodity would be warranted.

reading: CYP+E is a graded or differentiated variety of cyperus, counted in medium whole figures with fractions at an ordinary rate.
why: It co-occurs overwhelmingly with CYP (6 times) and NI (10 times), the classic cyperus-and-NI pairing of staple accounting; its fraction rate (36%) is close to the corpus staple norm and well above the bulk-commodity pattern; and its largest figure (20) is modest, consistent with measured staple quantities rather than bulk grain or livestock tallies.
refuted_by: If CYP+E were found systematically listed alongside VIR or sex-disaggregated counts, or if its figures were consistently sub-unit fractions only with no whole-number entries, the staple reading would be undermined.

reading: NA is a staple commodity, likely a foodstuff such as figs, olives, or a similar agricultural product, recorded in modest whole-number quantities with fractions at the ordinary rate.

refuted_by: If NA were found consistently recorded in large figures (dozens or hundreds) without fractions, or if it were shown to appear only as an addendum ligated to another sign rather than as a free-standing commodity entry, the staple reading would be false.

reading: MA is a staple commodity—likely a foodstuff such as figs, olives, or a similar agricultural product—recorded in moderate quantities across multiple palatial sites.

reading: DA marks a valued commodity recorded in small quantities with fractional amounts, consistent with a precious or rare good such as a spice, aromatic, or metal.

refuted_by: If DA were found in documents with large whole-number figures and no fractions, or listed alongside livestock or grain tallies in bulk quantities, the fine-commodity reading would be false.

reading: *188 is a valued commodity recorded in small quantities with fractions, likely a spice, aromatic, or similar high-value good.
why: The largest figure is only 13, which is small; fractions appear in 50% of the documents with figures, well above the 27% corpus base rate for commodity signs; and it appears after GRA and NI as a sub-quantity (smaller figure than the preceding commodity), consistent with a minor valued additive rather than a bulk staple.
refuted_by: If future tablets showed *188 recorded in large whole-number quantities (e.g., figures in the hundreds) without fractions, the fine-commodity reading would be false and a bulk or staple class would be required instead.

reading: *516 is a staple commodity, likely a plant product such as cyperus or a similar agricultural good, recorded in whole units across administrative contexts at multiple palatial sites.
why: The single attested figure is accompanied by fractions (100% fraction rate against a 27% base rate is based on only 1 figure, so this is weak, but fractions do appear, consistent with staple rather than bulk or fine); it appears on stone vessels and roundels as well as tablets, a support profile matching commodity recording; and it co-occurs with CYP (cyperus) and GRA (grain), placing it firmly in the agricultural commodity cluster.
refuted_by: If *516 were found consistently preceding or following a figure that sums other entries (functioning like KU-RO), or if it appeared repeatedly without any accompanying numeral, the staple reading would be false and a heading or total classification would be required instead.

reading: *401+RU is a staple commodity, likely a plant product or processed good, recorded in small-to-medium quantities alongside cyperus, olive products, and similar staples.
why: It co-occurs repeatedly with CYP (cyperus, 4 times) and NI (figs, 3 times) and OLE (olive, 1 time), all canonical staple commodities; it follows CYP and OLE in entry order, consistent with a commodity listed in sequence with peers rather than heading or summing them; fractions appear in 100% of entries with figures, which is above the 27% base rate but not extreme, fitting the staple class better than bulk (which rarely takes fractions) or fine (which would show very small figures with high fraction rates).
refuted_by: If future tablets show *401+RU appearing before a summing total that aggregates entries of CYP or NI, or if it is found qualifying another sign as a ligature component rather than standing as an independent entry with its own figure, the staple reading would be undermined.

reading: KU-PA₃-NU is a totalling word that precedes or accompanies a summed figure in the account.
why: It co-occurs overwhelmingly with KU-RO (5 times) and KI-RO (3 times), both well-known Linear A totalling/balancing terms, placing it firmly in the accounting summary vocabulary; it never appears with a commodity figure of its own ("with a figure: never"); and it never opens a tablet (0 of 8 in first position), consistent with a word that appears inside or at the close of an entry rather than as a heading.
refuted_by: If a tablet were found showing KU-PA₃-NU followed directly by a numeral with no intervening KU-RO or KI-RO, and especially if it appeared in first position opening a new section, the totalling reading would be undermined.

reading: RU is a label or transaction term that opens or titles a record, not a counted commodity.
why: It appears in first position on a tablet at a rate (1 of 5, 20%) well above the corpus base rate (11%), suggesting a document-opening role; it carries figures only twice across 8 attestations and never with fractions, which is inconsistent with a commodity being tallied; and it appears across diverse support types (tablet, stone vessel, 4-sided bar) and four sites, suggesting a functional administrative term rather than a site-specific commodity.
refuted_by: If RU were found consistently following a total-marker or appearing mid-tablet after a list of entries with accumulating figures, its heading role would be falsified and a commodity or total reading would be preferred instead.

reading: A valued commodity, likely a processed or graded derivative of olive oil or grain, recorded in small fractional amounts as a sub-quantity of a preceding commodity entry.
why: Fractions appear in 80% of attestations with figures (far above the 27% corpus base rate for commodity signs), the largest figure is only 30, and in the one case where a preceding commodity figure is available the QA2+[?]+PU figure is smaller — a classic sub-quantity pattern consistent with a costly or refined product drawn from a bulk commodity.
refuted_by: If future attestations show QA2+[?]+PU consistently recorded in large whole-number figures without fractions, or appearing independently of bulk commodity entries rather than after OLE or GRA, the fine-commodity reading would be falsified.

reading: MI+JA+RU is a valued commodity recorded in small quantities with a high rate of fractional amounts, consistent with a spice, aromatic, or similar fine good.
why: The largest figure is only 4, indicating small quantities typical of fine commodities; fractions appear in 60% of attestations with figures, more than double the corpus base rate of 27%, strongly suggesting a high-value commodity measured precisely; it appears alongside CYP (cyperus, an aromatic) and OLE (oil), company consistent with fine or aromatic goods.
refuted_by: If MI+JA+RU were found recorded in large whole-number quantities (e.g., figures in the dozens or hundreds) without fractions, the fine-commodity reading would be falsified.

reading: QE is a syllabic sign added to commodity logograms to mark a subtype or grade of the commodity.
why: It is attested as an added syllable attached to at least five different signs (*307, DI, GRA, JU, PA3), which is the defining behaviour of a qualifier; it never opens a tablet (0 of 6, against an 11% base rate), making it unlikely to be a heading or total; and it co-occurs with commodity signs (GRA, VIN, CYP) rather than appearing as a standalone counted item.
refuted_by: If QE were found standing alone before a numeral, without attachment to any logogram or commodity sign, across multiple documents, it would cease to be a qualifier and would need reclassification as a commodity or name.

reading: SU is a staple commodity, likely a plant product or processed foodstuff, recorded in moderate whole-number quantities with fractions at a rate consistent with ordinary staple goods.
why: The largest figure is only 12, consistent with staple-scale rather than bulk-grain quantities; fractions appear in 1 of 6 figured entries (17%), close to the corpus staple rate and not suppressed as in bulk commodities; it co-occurs with CYP (cyperus, a known staple) and VIN (wine), suggesting a commodity context rather than a personnel or textile list.
refuted_by: If SU were found consistently in large figures (hundreds or thousands) with fractions near zero, or if it appeared exclusively attached to other signs as a ligature qualifier rather than standing alone with its own figures, the staple reading would be false.

reading: NE is a label or transaction word that opens a tablet record, not a counted commodity.
why: It appears in first position on 2 of 7 tablets (29%), far above the 11% base rate for all units, signalling a document-opening function; it is attested on only 8 documents across four sites with no consistent large figures, unlike a commodity; and it appears on a metal object as well as tablets, consistent with a label rather than a tally entry.
refuted_by: If NE were found consistently in mid-tablet position following other entries, or if it accumulated large summed figures under a KU-RO total, it would cease to look like a heading and would need reclassification as a commodity or name.

reading: VIR+KA denotes a category of male persons, distinguished from plain VIR by the added syllable KA, counted in whole units and recorded in administratively significant quantities.
why: The base sign is VIR (the standard male-person logogram); figures are whole numbers with no fractions (0% vs. 27% corpus base rate), consistent with counting persons; the largest figure of 82 is in the range typical of personnel tallies rather than small commodity lots.
refuted_by: If VIR+KA were found recorded alongside fractional quantities, or if the sign appeared in contexts where livestock or commodity signs dominate without any personnel vocabulary, the persons reading would be undermined.

reading: DA-RE is a transaction or record label that opens or frames an entry, functioning as an administrative heading rather than a commodity or party.
why: It never appears with a figure of its own; it appears after GRA (a grain commodity sign), suggesting it labels or qualifies the record rather than being counted itself; it is never in first position on a tablet (0/6), which is unusual for a heading but consistent with a section label within a document rather than an opening title, and its co-occurrence with totalling words like KU-RO and PO-TO-KU-RO suggests it sits inside structured accounting blocks as a category marker.
refuted_by: If DA-RE were found accompanied by its own numeral in a list alongside other commodities or persons, it would cease to be a heading and would instead be a commodity or name entry.

reading: SE is a bare syllable added to commodity signs to mark a subtype or grade of the commodity.
why: It is attested as an added syllable attached to DA, RE, and SI, which is the defining behaviour of a qualifier; it never appears with a figure of its own in a first-position heading role (0 of 4 tablets); and it lacks a shared Linear B sign entry, consistent with a functional rather than lexical logogram.

reading: SI-RU-TE is a party name — a person or place — recorded as a list entry on stone vessels at multiple sanctuary sites.

reading: MA-DI is a personal or place name entered as a party in administrative records, most likely identifying an individual or locality associated with transactions at Haghia Triada and Phaistos.
why: The identical sequence exists in Linear B as a personal name, providing the strongest parallel; it never appears with a commodity figure of its own and never opens a tablet (ruling out heading or total); it co-occurs with KU-RO (a known totalling word) and PA-I-TO (the place name Phaistos), the pattern typical of named parties in an account rather than a commodity entry.
refuted_by: If MA-DI were found consistently preceding or following a numeral with a commodity ideogram (especially with fractional quantities or a species sign), it would indicate a commodity or staple rather than a name.

refuted_by: If future tablets showed *304+PA recorded in large whole-number figures (tens or hundreds) without fractions, the fine-commodity reading would be false and a bulk or staple class would need to be considered instead.

reading: GRA+F is a valued commodity recorded in small fractional amounts, likely a grade or variety of grain distinguished by the added syllable F.
why: Fractions appear in 100% of the figured attestations, far above the 27% base rate for commodity signs, which is the hallmark of a fine or precious commodity; the largest figure is only 70, consistent with small-quantity recording; it is a ligature (base GRA + added sign), the standard way Linear A marks a graded or distinguished sub-type of a commodity.
refuted_by: If future tablets show GRA+F recorded consistently in large whole-number quantities without fractions, at the scale typical of bulk staple grain, the fine-commodity reading would be falsified.

reading: A-RI is a bare syllabic element added to commodity signs as a modifier or grade marker, not itself a counted commodity.
why: It never appears with a figure (0 of 3 attestations), which rules out any counted commodity class; it never opens a tablet (0% vs 11% base rate), which argues against heading; and its three occurrences are spread across two sites on tablet supports, consistent with a recurring adjectival or qualifying element attached to other signs rather than standing as an independent entry.
refuted_by: If any tablet were found showing A-RI followed directly by a numeral or fraction, it would demonstrate it is a counted commodity rather than a qualifier.

reading: ME is a bare syllable added to commodity signs to mark a grade, type, or processing state of the commodity recorded.
why: ME appears as an added syllable attached to OLE and SI rather than standing alone with its own figures; it never appears with a figure of its own; it is attested on stone vessel supports, consistent with labelling commodity containers rather than counting independent items.
refuted_by: If ME were found standing alone at the head of an entry followed by a numeral, with no host logogram, it would cease to be a qualifier and would require reclassification as a commodity or name.

reading: JE is a label or transaction word that opens a document, marking the record type or administrative category of what follows.
why: It appears in first position on a tablet in 1 of 2 tablet attestations (50%), far above the 11% base rate for all units; it carries a figure only once and that figure is small (2), consistent with a label rather than a counted commodity; it has no fractions, which fits a non-commodity function.
refuted_by: If JE were found consistently mid-tablet following other entries, or if it appeared with a range of larger figures summed by a total word, it would not be a heading.

reading: *401+RO is a type of textile commodity, with the added syllable RO marking a specific grade or variety of the base cloth sign.
why: It is a ligature (base sign + added syllable RO), which is the structural hallmark of textile logograms that use added signs to specify type; it appears with a figure of 1 (whole unit, no fractions), consistent with textiles counted in whole units; the zero fraction rate (vs. 27% corpus base rate) further supports a whole-unit commodity rather than a liquid or fine commodity.
refuted_by: If *401+RO were found recorded in large figures, accompanied by fractional amounts, or listed alongside confirmed textile signs in a way that made it clearly a different commodity class, the textile reading would be undermined.

reading: A-MA is a party name (person or place) appearing as a list entry associated with a recorded quantity on administrative objects.
why: It appears only 3 times across 3 different sites and 3 different support types (bar, stone vessel, stone object), suggesting it labels a party rather than a commodity class; it never appears with a commodity figure-sign that would identify it as a staple or livestock entry; the small, scattered attestation count is consistent with a named party rather than a recurring commodity term.
refuted_by: If A-MA were found consistently preceding or following a known commodity ideogram (grain, oil, livestock) with regular fractional or whole-number tallies across multiple tablets, it would indicate a commodity or qualifier rather than a name.

reading: A-JA is a label or transaction term that opens a document, functioning as a record or category header rather than a counted commodity or named party.
why: It appears in first position on its one tablet (1 of 1, against an 11% base rate, making initial position its defining feature); it is never accompanied by a figure, which rules out commodity or name entries that require a numeral; and its spread across three different document types and sites (tablet, inked inscription, stone vessel) suggests a functional administrative word rather than a site-specific commodity or personal name.
refuted_by: If a tablet were found showing A-JA followed directly by a numeral and a commodity ideogram, it would demonstrate that A-JA is a counted item rather than a heading.

reading: *412+E is a type of textile, distinguished from related cloth types by the added syllable E, recorded in small whole-number quantities at Malia.
why: All three attestations carry whole-number figures with no fractions (0%), consistent with textiles counted in discrete units; the largest figure is only 4, typical of textile tallies rather than bulk staples; the sign is a ligature with an added syllable, the standard formation for textile-type distinctions in Linear A administration.
refuted_by: If fractional quantities were found alongside *412+E in further documents, or if the sign appeared in species-by-sex lists or alongside VIR, the textile reading would be undermined.

reading: QI+SI is a type of textile, with the added syllable SI specifying a variety or grade of the base cloth commodity.
why: Figures are small (max 5) and always whole with no fractions (0%), consistent with counted textile units; it is a ligature (base sign + added syllable), the standard formation for textile type-marking in Linear A administration; it appears exclusively on stone vessel supports at Zakros alongside *22F (a known textile-associated logogram) and RA, a combination that fits a textile accounting context.
refuted_by: If QI+SI were found recorded with fractional quantities, or in large figures typical of bulk staples, or consistently alongside liquid/grain logograms rather than textile-class signs, the textile reading would be undermined.

reading: DU-RE-ZA-SE is a party—a person or place—entered in stone-vessel accounts at Zakros alongside a figure.
why: All three attestations are on stone vessels at a single site (Zakros), a context typical of named parties or commodities in administrative records; it never appears in first position, ruling out a heading; and its co-occurring units (PA, DA-I-PI-TA, *131B) are consistent with a list of named entries rather than commodity classifiers or totalling words.
refuted_by: If DU-RE-ZA-SE were found consistently preceding or following a known commodity sign with varying quantities across multiple sites, it would be better read as a commodity or qualifier rather than a name.
